mean: to gasp in awe or shock
lit: to swallow one's breath: the sharp intake of air at a sudden sight

use.how: Reaction to something seen or heard that is stunning, shocking or tense: 景色に息を呑んだ. Often before a noun: 息を呑むほど美しい, 息を呑む接戦.

near.diff: 目を見張る is being impressed by how remarkable something is, such as progress or skill; 息を呑む is a sudden gasp at beauty, shock or suspense.
息が詰まる is feeling stifled by a tense or oppressive atmosphere over time; 息を呑む is a momentary gasp.

ctx.en: The sunrise seen from the summit was so beautiful that I caught my breath without meaning to.

ctx.s: 事故[じこ]の映像[えいぞう]が流[なが]れると、会場[かいじょう]の全員[ぜんいん]が{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
ctx.en: When the footage of the accident was shown, everyone in the hall gasped.

ctx.s: 「最後[さいご]のシーン、{息[いき]を呑[の]む}ほどきれいだったね。」
ctx.en: "That last scene was breathtakingly beautiful, wasn't it?"

ctx.s: ドアを開[あ]けた瞬間[しゅんかん]、彼女[かのじょ]は荒[あ]らされた部屋[へや]を見[み]て{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
ctx.en: The moment she opened the door, she saw the ransacked room and gasped.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]は最後[さいご]まで{息[いき]を呑[の]む}接戦[せっせん]が続[つづ]いた。
ctx.en: The match stayed a breathtakingly close contest right to the end.

ctx.s: 観客[かんきゃく]は{息[いき]を呑[の]んで}綱渡[つなわた]りを見守[みまも]った。
ctx.en: The audience watched the tightrope walk with bated breath.

bad.s: ジョギングのあと、ベンチに座[すわ]って{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: after jogging I sat on a bench and got my breath back)
bad.why: It is a gasp at something striking, not recovering after exercise. Getting your breath back is iki o totonoeru or hitoiki tsuku.

bad.s: 怒[おこ]られるのが怖[こわ]くて、言[い]いたいことを{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: I was afraid of being told off, so I swallowed what I wanted to say)
bad.why: Holding back your words is kotoba o nomikomu. Iki o nomu takes no other object and is a gasp, not self-restraint.

mean: win or lose, staking everything on a gamble
lit: 'one or eight': a gambler's all-or-nothing call on how things will fall

use.how: Adverb before a risky move (一か八かやってみる, 一か八か勝負に出る) or before a noun: 一か八かの賭け. Said when success is a toss-up and there is no safer option.

near.diff: 思い切って just means boldly taking the plunge; 一か八か stresses that it could fail completely and the result is down to luck.

ctx.s: もう時間[じかん]がない。{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}やってみよう。

ctx.en: He put all his savings in and staked everything on one throw.

ctx.s: 「間[ま]に合[あ]わないかもしれないけど、{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}走[はし]ってみる！」

ctx.s: 残[のこ]り数秒[すうびょう]、彼[かれ]は{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}遠[とお]くからシュートを放[はな]った。
ctx.en: With seconds left, he took a do-or-die shot from long range.

ctx.en: Applying only to your first-choice university is an all-or-nothing gamble.

ctx.en: I took a chance and confessed my feelings, and to my amazement we ended up going out.

bad.en: (meant: I get up at seven or eight every morning)

mean: taking one's anger out on innocent people
lit: striking out in all eight directions: hitting whoever happens to be near

use.how: Noun, usually 〜に八つ当たりする or それは八つ当たりだ: venting anger caused by one thing on a person or object that had nothing to do with it.

near.diff: 逆恨み is resenting someone who did you no wrong, often the very person who helped or warned you; 八つ当たり is venting anger from elsewhere on whoever is nearby.

ctx.s: 「ごめん、さっきのはただの{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}だった。」
ctx.en: "Sorry, I was only taking it out on you back there."

ctx.s: 上司[じょうし]に叱[しか]られた父[ちち]は、帰[かえ]ってくるなり家族[かぞく]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}した。
ctx.en: After being scolded by his boss, my father came home and immediately took it out on the family.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は物[もの]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}して、ドアを思[おも]い切[き]り閉[し]めた。

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}する客[きゃく]を見[み]ると、嫌[いや]な気分[きぶん]になる。
ctx.en: Seeing customers take their bad mood out on shop staff makes me feel awful.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は「私[わたし]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}されても困[こま]るよ」とため息[いき]をついた。

bad.en: (meant: he got angry at the friend who broke the promise)

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじで{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}して、大金[たいきん]を手[て]に入[い]れた。
bad.en: (meant: I hit the jackpot in the lottery and won a fortune)

lit: knowing it a hundred times over

use.how: Predicate, usually 〜は百も承知だ or 〜を百も承知で: stresses that one is fully aware of a risk or objection, often before going ahead anyway.

near.diff: 承知の上 plainly says something was done knowingly; 百も承知 is more emphatic and often impatient: I know that perfectly well.

ctx.en: I know perfectly well it's dangerous. I still want to go.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は反対[はんたい]されるのを{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}で、会議[かいぎ]で意見[いけん]を述[の]べた。

ctx.s: 甘[あま]い物[もの]が体[からだ]に悪[わる]いのは{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}なのに、つい食[た]べてしまう。
ctx.en: I know perfectly well that sweets are bad for me, but I end up eating them anyway.

ctx.s: 無理[むり]なお願[ねが]いなのは{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}ですが、もう一度[いちど]ご検討[けんとう]いただけませんか。
ctx.en: I am fully aware this is a difficult request, but could you possibly reconsider?

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は批判[ひはん]が出[で]るのを{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}の上[うえ]で、若手[わかて]を起用[きよう]した。
ctx.en: Fully aware that he would be criticised, the manager picked the young players.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]、明日[あした]の集合時間[しゅうごうじかん]、{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}しました。
bad.en: (meant: Understood, sir, about tomorrow's meeting time)

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は本[ほん]をたくさん読[よ]むので、何[なん]でも{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}な人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he reads a lot, so he is very knowledgeable)
bad.why: It is about being fully aware of one particular fact, not about knowing a lot. A well-informed person is monoshiri.

mean: to stubbornly refuse to give in
lit: to hold one's pride stretched taut, refusing to let it bend

near.diff: 意地になる is getting fixated on doing something to prove a point; 意地を張る is refusing to concede, apologise or accept help.

ctx.s: 本当[ほんとう]は寂[さび]しいのに、彼[かれ]は{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}「一人[ひとり]で平気[へいき]だ」と言[い]った。
ctx.en: He was actually lonely, but out of pride he insisted he was fine on his own.

ctx.s: 道[みち]に迷[まよ]ったのに、父[ちち]は{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}誰[だれ]にも道[みち]を聞[き]かなかった。
ctx.en: We were lost, but my father stubbornly refused to ask anyone for directions.

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]とも{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}、一週間[いっしゅうかん]も口[くち]をきかなかった。
ctx.en: Neither of them would give in, and they didn't speak for a whole week.

bad.en: (meant: he perseveres with practice every day for his dream)

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{意地[いじ]を張[は]る}人[ひと]で、よく他人[たにん]の悪口[わるくち]を言[い]う。
bad.en: (meant: she is a mean person who often badmouths others)

lit: one's spirit sinks inward and down

near.diff: 気が重い is dread about something you have to do; 気が滅入る is a general gloom brought on by your surroundings or circumstances.

bad.en: (meant: the TV noise distracts me so I can't concentrate on studying)

mean: for one's attention to slacken without meaning to
lit: one's mind goes slack, like a string that has loosened

use.how: Predicate about attention or discipline relaxing, often after success, near the end or once used to something: 慣れて気が緩む. Usually explains a mistake or warns against one.

near.diff: 気が抜ける is feeling deflated and flat once tension is gone; 気が緩む is attention slackening, which tends to cause mistakes.
気を抜く is choosing to relax or ease off; 気が緩む happens to you without your meaning it.

ctx.en: With a big lead, perhaps their focus slipped without their noticing, because they gave up three goals near the end.

ctx.en: When I learned that the light from that star left it tens of thousands of years ago, my mind boggled.

bad.en: (meant: we've drifted apart lately and hardly talk)

mean: to feel a twinge of guilt
lit: one's own mind finds fault: the heart reproaches itself

near.diff: 気が引ける is hesitating because something feels awkward or presumptuous; 気がとがめる is guilt because you feel you have done something a little wrong.

ctx.en: I turned down my friend's invitation with a made-up excuse, and it's nagging at me a little.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]がとがめた}のか、次[つぎ]の日[ひ]に自分[じぶん]から謝[あやま]りに来[き]た。
ctx.en: Perhaps his conscience pricked him, because the next day he came to apologise of his own accord.

ctx.s: 母[はは]の誕生日[たんじょうび]を忘[わす]れていたのが{気[き]がとがめて}、花[はな]を買[か]って帰[かえ]った。
ctx.en: Feeling guilty that I'd forgotten my mother's birthday, I bought flowers on the way home.

mean: to be unable to fathom why anyone would do that

use.how: Usually 〜する人の気が知れない or Xの気が知れない: says another person's choice is beyond understanding, with clear disapproval.

near.diff: 首をかしげる is being puzzled or doubtful about something; 気が知れない bluntly rejects another person's choice as incomprehensible.

cue: Your neighbour drives an hour every weekend to queue overnight for limited-edition trainers, then never wears them. You say what you think of it.

ctx.s: こんなに寒[さむ]い日[ひ]に海[うみ]で泳[およ]ぐ人[ひと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
ctx.en: I can't understand people who swim in the sea on a day this cold.

ctx.s: 「三時間[さんじかん]も並[なら]んでラーメンを食[た]べるの？{気[き]が知[し]れない}な。」
ctx.en: "Queue for three hours for a bowl of ramen? I don't get it."

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]の前日[ぜんじつ]に徹夜[てつや]でゲームをするなんて、弟[おとうと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
ctx.en: Gaming all night the day before an exam? I can't fathom what my brother is thinking.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は「道[みち]にごみを捨[す]てる人[ひと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}」といつも怒[おこ]っている。
ctx.en: My grandfather is always grumbling, "I'll never understand people who drop litter in the street."

ctx.s: お金[かね]を払[はら]ってまで怖[こわ]い思[おも]いをしに行[い]く人[ひと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
ctx.en: I can't see why anyone would pay money just to be scared.

ctx.s: あんな条件[じょうけん]で契約[けいやく]にサインした社長[しゃちょう]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}と、社員[しゃいん]たちはあきれた。
ctx.en: The staff were appalled; they couldn't fathom why the president had signed a contract on those terms.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の天気[てんき]はまだ{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
bad.en: (meant: tomorrow's weather is still unknown)
bad.why: It is about another person's baffling choice, not about facts that are unknown. Say mada wakaranai.

bad.s: 新[あたら]しい先生[せんせい]は来[き]たばかりで、まだ{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
bad.en: (meant: the new teacher has only just arrived, so we don't know what they're like)
bad.why: It is not 'not yet known'; it condemns someone's choice as incomprehensible. Say donna hito ka mada wakaranai.
